R1887.summary: Written after the victory at Nördlingen: the other side is expected to spare no attempt to restore the princes who put themselves under its protection, above all Württemberg and Durlach, and Ferdinand asks the Cardinal-Infante to oppose the designs of the enemies of the House by a movement and diversion of his arms. A 6-token word and a 16-token span remain open.
R1887.en:
Since the common concern of establishing the welfare of our most august House requires above all ... one may easily
gather that he will not leave off any [attempts] that he believes will serve to restore those princes who have thrown
themselves on his faith and protection, above all the Württemberger and the Durlacher. And the [outcome] (crisdus) from
it will bring no less profit or harm to Your Dilection's affairs than to my [side?]. Therefore, since for my part I shall
not cease to strive to overturn these attempts of the enemies of our common House, I have thought it most necessary to
rouse the same zeal in Your Dilection, asking you most kindly that, by means of someone who, their minds being drawn off
in different directions, more easily for me to carry through this and their (... 16 tokens ...)

R1889.summary: The Cardinal-Infante refuses imperial winter quarters in the archbishopric and city of Trier, which has been under Spanish protection and garrison for two hundred years, and asks that the Spanish garrison keep the town and its surroundings for its own and the Elector's upkeep. Key recovered from the draft R954.
R1889.en:
As to the winter quarters, [which Your Royal Dignity and Dilection] desires to be made for the said imperial army in the
archbishopric and city of Trier ... But since the city of Trier has for two hundred years stood under the protection [of
His Royal Catholic Majesty], and [on that account] has been furnished with a garrison by his soldiers [whenever necessity
required it], [as it also was when] the Frenchman, overcoming the royal banners, occupied it, [I think it fitting that]
this royal garrison [be kept] in the said city and the surrounding places, [from which] it will draw the necessary
sustenance, [both for] itself, as is fitting, and for the upkeep of the Prince Elector (who until now has been provided
for from the treasury [of His Royal Catholic Majesty]). [...]

R1890.summary: Ferdinand III answers the new levies of the Elector of Cologne and the Westphalian circle: Count Hatzfeldt is to go to Cologne and raise a larger force, and the Cardinal-Infante is asked again for the hundred thousand florins, to be consigned at Cologne to the imperial commissaries; the Spanish envoy, the marques de Castaneda, will explain further.
R1890.en:
The ambassador of the Most Serene Catholic King, the Marquis of Castañeda, will communicate to Your Dilection what we
have discussed with him at greater length concerning the new levy of soldiers begun in the Westphalian Circle by the
Elector of Cologne and the estates of that Circle, and the disadvantages we fear from it to the prejudice of the public
good and also of our House. Since that business therefore needs a swift remedy, and no other means presents itself than
that we too should hastily set up in those parts a levy of soldiers that would extend to a larger number than the said
levy, if we wish otherwise to keep free disposal there and to take care that that Circle is not subjected to another's
will, we have therefore ordered that Count Hatzfeldt should transfer himself at once to Cologne and set his hand to this
work with all the speed he can.
